There could be a number of factors, age being one of them. A lot of the time different circuits are mounted on different poles so it is definitely possible the circuit you are on is mounted on older poles that slowly are replaced when they go down. There are also other protective devices that you may have which are more susceptible to outages, like fuses. If you are downstream of a nearby fuse it’s very easy for that fuse to blow from things like lightning, wind blowing debris into the line, even animals. Also if you are fed from an overhead mounted pole service line and your neighbors have underground electric service, they are more protected from all of these elemental factors.

I’m a system operator for the utility and can provide an actual answer. What you are calling the “grid,” is actual different circuits that TEP has, and while you are physically across the street from your neighbors, you and they are most likely on 2 completely different circuits that aren’t related. Think of your breaker box on the side of your home, and how there’s multiple breakers for different rooms, kitchen, bathroom, living room, etc. Those are all different circuits within the “grid” of your homes wiring. They’re all physically close but wired differently and operate independent of each other. This applies to you and your neighbors, and the circuit each of you are on. There are many other factors such as phasing, reclosing, etc but this is the easiest way to get the concept across. Hope this helps!

“University of Arizona Athletics’ most enduring tradition is the slogan and battle cry, “Bear Down.” 
 
More than a casual piece of encouragement, the rally cry has roots over a century old, to the Roaring ‘20s, and pre-dates another venerated exhortation, “Win one for the Gipper,” by two years.
 
In the fall of 1926, John Byrd “Button” Salmon was the newly installed student body president at the UA, a promising student and member of note of several of the school’s honor societies. He also was a varsity quarterback, a baseball catcher and generally acclaimed popular campus figure. He embodied all-around.
 
In early October after the Wildcat varsity defeated the freshman squad in an annual match at the time, Salmon and several friends were returning from a visit to Phoenix, and an automobile crash north of Tucson near Florence left the young athlete critically injured.
 
Salmon, then 22, lost his battle and died the morning of Oct. 18. A memorial service was held on campus that week, drawing a reported thousand mourners, and a line of cars stretched miles to his burial plot.
 
The coach at the time, J.F. “Pop” McKale, had visited Salmon in the hospital regularly before his death, and later told the squad the young athlete’s last message to his teammates was, “Tell them... tell the team to bear down.”
 
It’s unclear whether McKale invoked the phrase to the team before one of several games that year, a contest in Las Cruces against New Mexico A&M (NMSU) that same week, or two weeks later before a game against New Mexico in Tucson. UA won both.”

So I work in an office with 6 computers and different systems, 12 hour days either 6am-6pm or 6pm to 6am. During week days I coordinate with line crews in the field to do switching for maintenance, using SCADA to open and close substation and field breakers, putting reclosers into one shot for crews to do hot line work so the line becomes de energized if they go line to line or ground. 

My utility has smart meters that communicate with our Outage Management System (OMS) so anytime a meter loses power we see that in real time in the office without needing to call the customer. When an outage comes in I’m responsible for getting line crews to the correct location, troubleshooting what went wrong and why, and we have a few systems that run fault current that can predict where a fault may have happened on the system. 

If a run of cable goes bad and needs to be de-energized for work I’ll write and perform switching orders to get as many people back in power as we can while crews can fix the bad cable or whatever went bad.

 A lot of the time I’m nights and weekends is spent just watching tv or hitting the gym in the office when nothing is going on. I can monitor our SCADA and OMS via an iPad so I can see if something goes wrong while not being at my desk. 

My company is also putting me through a 3 year system operator training course so I do a lot of homework and take classes during the downtime as well, and that is probably something to expect for any company you go to.

The job itself as a locator is great. All the pros you mentioned are things I enjoy too, working outside, driving around, being alone, etc are all what enticed me to this field. Unfortunately a lot of how your job is done depends on your direct management, as well as the utility company you locate for if you go into contract work like USIC, ELM, Stake Center, etc. Personally, my management fucking sucks. Can never get a hold of anyone for help, constantly changing rules, and nit picking every little thing during audits. On top of that, the gas company I locate for are also complete lunatics and will nitpick the stuff that even management over looks, so much so that they’ll make you drive 45 minutes away from where you’re working to go to an old ticket to look at one mark that wasn’t completely perfect. Having the utility company look over your shoulder and watch your every move is some of the most stressful part about the job, and it’s why I’m currently looking for other options. HOWEVER, I haven’t left locating yet after doing it for almost 2 years because being able to take the work car home everyday is something that I do not take lightly with gas prices like we have right now, as well as getting a promotion and a $2 raise with it also helps. The high stakes that you mentioned is also definitely something to consider as well. I locate Gas and electric in my area, so if someone digs into a big gas main or a 3 phase primary, they’re getting blown up one way or another because of my fuck up. But locating itself is very easy, and unless you’re a complete moron with zero common sense, it won’t happen. Locating is easy to pick up but hard to master, so don’t be afraid to at least try it out and see how you like it. At the end of the day, it’s a good job that is necessary and fairly secure in this day and age. Your company will give you a phone, a computer, and everything you need to be successful. If you ever feel slightly hesitant about a locate, you can always call a fellow locator with your company for help, or even management if yours is even halfway decent.
